fetched_contents.text: Global burden of thyroid cancer in 2022: Incidence and mortality estimates from GLOBOCAN Abstract Background: Thyroid cancer (TC) is the most common malignancy of the endocrine system. This study aimed to assess the global distribution of TC incidence and mortality in 2022, as well as to predict the burden for the year 2050. Methods: Data from the GLOBOCAN 2022 database were used to analyze the age-standardized incidence and mortality rates of TC by sex, age group (<55 years and ≥55 years), country, world region, and level of Human Development Index (HDI) for 185 countries. The predicted incidence and mortality burden for 2050 was calculated based on demographic projections. Results: In 2022, an estimated 821,214 new TC cases and 47,507 TC-related deaths occurred worldwide. The age-standardized incidence rates (ASIRs) and age-standardized mortality rates (ASMRs) were higher in women (ASIR: 13.60 per 100,000; ASMR: 0.53 per 100,000) than in men (ASIR: 4.60 per 100,000; ASMR: 0.35 per 100,000). The ASIR in high HDI countries was approximately ten times higher than that in low HDI countries for both sexes, with relatively similar ASMR across regions. Among 185 countries, China had the largest number of TC cases (accounting for 56.77% of total cases) and TC-related deaths (accounting for 24.35% of global TC-related deaths), with the highest ASIR in men (13.30 per 100,000). Worldwide, approximately 64.63% of TC cases occurred in populations under 55 years old, while nearly 82.99% of TC-related deaths occurred in populations aged 55 years and above. If the rates stay the same as in 2022, it is projected that approximately 1,100,000 new TC cases and 91,000 TC-related deaths will occur in 2050, indicating a 34.15% and 89.58% increase, respectively. Conclusions: TC is a highly frequent cancer worldwide with disparities across regions, genders, and age groups. Our results provide light on the worldwide TC disease burden and facilitate regionally customized prevention measures. Such analyses may aid in developing personalized prevention and control strategies for TC. The widespread use of imaging techniques and the introduction of fine-needle aspiration biopsy have significantly improved the detection rate of TC. However, this has led to a growing concern regarding overdiagnosis.[9] Variations in the quality of medical and health services globally contribute to significant disparities in TC burden across countries. Assessing the burden of TC in different regions and specific countries can help to evaluate the fairness of health service resources and highlight the accessibility of diagnosis and treatment in nations with varying income levels. Previous studies on TC incidence and mortality have focused on specific countries, regions, or populations.[10–13] However, limited research examined the current global burden of TC using the most up-to-date data, especially in analyzing variations across different sex and age groups. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) provided detailed estimates of cancer prevalence through the Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN), allowing for comparisons of TC burden across countries and regions.[1] In this study, we aimed to assess the worldwide epidemiological landscape of TC in 2022, considering factors such as geography and socioeconomic status, and project the future burden of TC up to 2050 using the GLOBOCAN 2022 database. fetched_contents.text: Global patterns and trends in incidence and mortality of thyroid cancer in children and adolescents: a population-based study Summary Background There has been a considerable increase in thyroid cancer incidence among adults in several countries in the past three decades, attributed primarily to overdiagnosis. We aimed to assess global patterns and trends in incidence and mortality of thyroid cancer in children and adolescents, in view of the increased incidence among adults. Methods We did a population-based study of the observed incidence (in 49 countries and territories) and mortality (in 27 countries) of thyroid cancer in children and adolescents aged 0–19 years using data from the International Incidence of Childhood Cancer Volume 3 study database, the WHO mortality database, and the cancer incidence in five continents database (CI5plus; for adult data [age 20–74 years]). We analysed temporal trends in incidence rates, including absolute changes in rates, and the strength of the correlation between incidence rates in children and adolescents and in adults. We calculated the average annual number of thyroid cancer deaths and the age-standardised mortality rates for children and adolescents. Findings Age-standardised incidence rates of thyroid cancer among children and adolescents aged 0–19 years ranged from 0·4 (in Uganda and Kenya) to 13·4 (in Belarus) cancers per 1 million person-years in 2008–12. The variability in the incidence rates was mostly accounted for by the papillary tumour subtype. Incidence rates were almost always higher in girls than in boys and increased with age in both sexes. Rapid increases in incidence between 1998–2002 and 2008–12 were observed in almost all countries. Country-specific incidence rates in children and adolescents were strongly correlated (r>0·8) with rates in adults, as were the temporal changes in the respective incidence rates (r>0·6). Thyroid cancer deaths in those aged younger than 20 years were less than 0·1 per 10 million person-years in each country. Interpretation The pattern of thyroid cancer incidence in children and adolescents mirrors the pattern seen in adults, suggesting a major role for overdiagnosis, which, in turn, can lead to overtreatment, lifelong medical care, and side effects that can negatively affect quality of life. We suggest that the existing recommendation against screening for thyroid cancer in the asymptomatic adult population who are free from specific risk factors should be extended to explicitly recommend against screening for thyroid cancer in similar populations of children and adolescents. Introduction The epidemiological landscape of thyroid cancer has changed substantially since the 1990s. A marked increase in the incidence rates of thyroid cancer among adults has been recorded in many medium-resource and high-resource countries.1, 2 The disease is diagnosed more frequently in women, with a female-to-male age-standardised incidence rate (ASR) ratio ranging from 3 to 4, depending on the country analysed. Thyroid cancer has become the fifth most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide in adult women aged 20–84 years and the third most common in women aged younger than 50 years.3 Increasing incidence is primarily driven by the increase in the number of small papillary carcinomas,4, 5 while, by marked contrast, mortality rates are low and have remained stable or declined in most countries,6 indicating that the increase in incidence is largely due to overdiagnosis.1, 2, 5 Overdiagnosis is the detection of subclinical cancers that are unlikely to cause harm in a person's lifetime.7, 8, 9, 10 The increasing availability of non-invasive diagnostic techniques introduced in the late 1980s, such as ultrasound, CT, and MRI, and more recently PET scans,11 in combination with the use of fine-needle aspiration biopsies and changes in physicians' practice of investigating thyroid findings, has revealed a large number of subclinical cancers in the thyroid glands of adults and,8, 9 more recently, in adolescents.10 We aimed to analyse global patterns and trends in thyroid cancer incidence and mortality in children and adolescents and compare them with corresponding patterns in adults, using the most up-to-date international data, to test the hypothesis that overdiagnosis of thyroid cancer might be occurring not just in adults, but also among younger people. Evidence from a small number of countries has shown an increase in the incidence rates of thyroid cancer in children and adolescents. As the considerable increase in thyroid cancer incidence observed among adults worldwide has been attributed primarily to overdiagnosis, it is not clear whether the same phenomenon might also be present in younger populations. Age-specific incidence patterns in children and adolescents show a broad age trend: incidence is generally low in infancy and increases with age, with the strongest evidence pointing to a rise in adolescents and young adults, but the exact peak varies by study and region. The most direct evidence comes from the population-based study of children and adolescents aged 0–19 years, which reported age-standardized incidence rates ranging from 0.4 to 13.4 per 1 million person-years in 2008–2012, with incidence almost always higher in girls than in boys and increasing with age in both sexes [N1-F2]. This suggests a general upward trend across childhood age groups, but not a single universal peak in a single age range.

In infants, the evidence is less detailed than in older children. The CDC pediatric cancer report notes that pediatric cancer incidence was highest in children aged 0–4 years overall, but in some states the highest rates were among persons aged 15–19 years [N3-F3]. This implies that infants and very young children may have relatively lower rates compared with older children and adolescents, but the evidence is not strong enough to say that incidence is consistently lowest in infancy. The broader thyroid-cancer-specific evidence from N1-F2 also emphasizes that incidence increases with age, which is consistent with a general rise in older children and adolescents.

The age distribution across infants, children, and adolescents is therefore best described as: lowest in infancy, increasing in children, and rising further in adolescents, with the strongest observed increases in adolescents and young adults. The N1-F2 study explicitly states that incidence rates increase with age in both sexes, and the 2021 global data also highlight that the 20–24 age group bears a substantial thyroid cancer burden [N1-R2]. The N4 evidence adds that thyroid cancer incidence has increased across all age groups from 1995 to 2014 in the United States, including in the 0–14 and 15–24 groups [N4-R1]. Taken together, the most reliable evidence base for age patterns is the population-based childhood study and the broader global and national incidence evidence, which both support a generally increasing trend with age [N1-F2][N1-R2][N4-R1].

A key caveat is that the N1-F2 study explicitly notes that incidence rates were strongly correlated with adult rates and that temporal increases were observed almost everywhere, which suggests that the apparent age pattern may be influenced by secular trends rather than purely biological age effects [N1-F2]. Still, the age-specific pattern itself remains consistent across the evidence: incidence rises with age, with the steepest increases occurring in adolescents and young adults, and the lowest rates in infancy or the youngest age groups [N1-F2][N3-F3].

Gender differences in pediatric thyroid cancer incidence are consistent across the evidence: incidence is higher in girls than in boys. The population-based study of children and adolescents aged 0–19 years reports that incidence rates were almost always higher in girls than in boys, with girls consistently having higher rates than boys across all age groups [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN 2022 global cancer report also states that thyroid cancer is three to four times more common in women than in men and that the female-to-male age-standardized incidence rate ratio ranges from 3 to 4 depending on the country analyzed [N1-F1]. In addition, the Frontiers in Oncology article on pediatric and adolescent thyroid cancer notes that women account for a large proportion of cases and that the female-to-male incidence ratio is substantial [N1-R2]. Overall, the evidence strongly supports a female excess.

The possible explanations for the gender gap are primarily biological rather than solely demographic. The GLOBOCAN report explicitly links the higher incidence in women to biological factors and states that thyroid cancer is the only non-reproductive cancer that predominantly affects women [N1-F1]. The same report also notes that the female excess is “three to four times” greater than in men, which is consistent with hormonal and other biological mechanisms [N1-F1]. The Frontiers in Oncology article similarly frames the pattern as broadly consistent with a biological mechanism and attributes the higher incidence in girls to the same general principle that applies to adult women [N1-R2]. The N2 evidence further supports this by emphasizing that thyroid cancer is significantly less common in children than in adults and that the female-to-male ratio is large, though the excerpt does not provide detailed biological mechanisms [N2-R2]. The Mayo Clinic/Medscape summaries also note that women are three to four times more likely than men to be diagnosed with thyroid cancer, reinforcing the gender gap [N2-R5].

As for whether the gender gap changes with age, the evidence is more nuanced. The population-based childhood study states that incidence increases with age in both sexes, but it does not provide evidence that the female excess becomes larger or smaller with age [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN report likewise states that the female-to-male incidence ratio is consistent across regions and that the female excess is a major feature of thyroid cancer epidemiology [N1-F1]. The pediatric cancer geography report in the U.S. does not specifically discuss thyroid cancer gender differences, so it is not directly relevant to this point [N3-F3]. Thus, the most reliable conclusion is that girls consistently have higher incidence than boys, and the gender gap appears to be relatively stable across age groups, though the evidence does not support a strong change in the gap with age [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R5].

Study limitations also matter. The population-based childhood study notes that the pattern of incidence in children and adolescents mirrors the adult pattern and suggests overdiagnosis as a major explanation [N1-F2]. This implies that the gender difference may be influenced by diagnostic and reporting factors, including the increased use of imaging and biopsies, rather than being entirely biological. The GLOBOCAN report similarly points to overdiagnosis and improved detection as factors affecting thyroid cancer incidence in adults and notes that detection improvements can lead to higher apparent incidence [N1-F1]. Therefore, the gender gap should be interpreted cautiously and may include some diagnostic component, especially in the pediatric literature [N1-F2][N1-F1].

Geographic variation in pediatric thyroid cancer incidence is substantial, but the evidence base is uneven. The strongest direct evidence comes from the population-based childhood study, which reports age-standardized incidence rates ranging from 0.4 to 13.4 per 1 million person-years in 49 countries and territories, with the highest rate observed in Belarus and the lowest in Uganda and Kenya [N1-F2]. The global pediatric and adolescent thyroid cancer burden article also notes that the 20–24 age group bears a substantial thyroid cancer burden globally [N1-R2], suggesting that regional patterns are not confined to a single age group. In addition, the CDC pediatric cancer report indicates that pediatric cancer incidence was highest in the Northeast and lowest in the South in the United States, with highest rates in metropolitan areas with populations ≥1 million and counties in the top 25% economic status [N3-F3].

For continent and country-level variation, the evidence is mixed. The population-based childhood study provides country-level estimates but does not specify continents; however, the incidence range of 0.4–13.4 per 1 million person-years already suggests large variation across countries and regions [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN 2022 report states that age-standardized incidence rates in high HDI countries were approximately ten times higher than those in low HDI countries for both sexes [N1-F1]. This implies a major geographic gradient, with higher incidence in wealthier regions. The CDC U.S. report also shows state-level variation, with incidence rates ranging from 145 to 206 per million and highest in New Hampshire, the District of Columbia, and New Jersey [N3-F3]. It also notes that incidence rates were highest in the Northeast and lowest in the South [N3-F3]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that incidence differs by continent and country, with high HDI regions having much higher incidence than low HDI regions, and within the U.S. incidence differs by Census region and state [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Urban/rural differences are also evident. The CDC report notes that pediatric cancer incidence was higher in metropolitan areas with populations ≥1 million than in nonmetropolitan areas [N3-F3]. This is consistent with the broader point in the N3 evidence that increased use of medical imaging may lead to geographic differences in thyroid cancer incidence through enhanced detection of low-risk lesions [N3-R4]. The population-based childhood study does not specifically address urban/rural variation, so that conclusion is limited to the CDC evidence [N3-F3].

The geographic patterns suggest several possible environmental or diagnostic influences. First, the CDC report explicitly ties geographic differences in pediatric cancer incidence to increased use of medical imaging and improved detection, with the implication that some geographic variation reflects better diagnosis rather than true biological variation [N3-R4]. Second, the GLOBOCAN report notes that the female excess and overdiagnosis are major epidemiological features, and that improved detection and imaging have increased apparent incidence [N1-F1]. Third, the population-based childhood study points to papillary tumor subtype as explaining much of the variability in incidence rates [N1-F2]. Finally, the radiation-related evidence suggests that environmental exposure, especially radiation, can increase thyroid cancer risk [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Taken together, the geographic variation is best interpreted as a combination of real biological and environmental factors, plus diagnostic and detection-related factors, with better access to imaging and biopsies likely amplifying apparent differences [N3-R4][N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4].

Study quality and limitations are important for interpreting pediatric thyroid cancer incidence. Registry methods and case ascertainment affect estimates in two main ways: first, the quality of source registries influences whether a region’s incidence is overestimated or underestimated, and second, the completeness of case ascertainment determines whether incidence is measured accurately. The GLOBOCAN 2022 report states that the reliability of cancer data at the national level depends on the representativeness and quality of the source information, and that the methods used in compiling cancer estimates are consistent with those used in previous studies [N1-F1]. The same report notes that national cancer registries and vital registries provided the best available recorded data, while the reliability of data depends on source quality [N1-F1]. The population-based childhood study similarly uses population-based cancer data from the International Incidence of Childhood Cancer Volume 3 study, the WHO mortality database, and the CI5plus database, which implies that these data are intended to be high-quality but still subject to registry limitations [N1-F2].

Diagnostic criteria and age/gender definitions also vary across studies. The population-based childhood study reports age-standardized incidence rates and uses person-years of follow-up, which is a standard method for incidence estimation [N1-F2]. However, the GLOBOCAN report explicitly notes that incidence rates were higher in women than in men and that the female-to-male ASIR ratio varies by country, indicating that age and sex definitions may not be identical across all studies [N1-F1]. The CDC pediatric cancer report likewise uses age-adjusted rates and reports incidence by sex, race/ethnicity, state, Census region, and county-level economic status [N3-F3]. The N4 evidence includes incidence trends from U.S. cancer registries and notes that incidence increased across all age groups from 1995 to 2014, but it does not provide enough detail on diagnostic criteria for thyroid cancer specifically [N4-R1]. The N6 evidence adds that imaging and radiation exposure may contribute to increased incidence, which is relevant to case ascertainment but not directly to diagnostic criteria [N6-R5].

The most reliable evidence base for each subgroup is therefore uneven. For age patterns, the population-based childhood study provides the strongest direct evidence, because it is explicitly population-based and covers children and adolescents aged 0–19 years [N1-F2]. For gender differences, the GLOBOCAN report and the Frontiers in Oncology article provide the most reliable cross-population evidence, because they report age-standardized incidence ratios and global patterns [N1-F1][N1-R2]. For geographic variation, the CDC pediatric cancer report is the most reliable regional and country-level source because it provides state-level estimates and detailed geographic breakdowns [N3-F3]. For radiation and environmental influences, the N6 evidence is strongest because it directly links radiation exposure and imaging to thyroid cancer incidence [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

Overall, the evidence supports a cautious interpretation: registry quality and ascertainment affect incidence estimates, diagnostic criteria and age/sex definitions are not always identical across studies, and the most reliable evidence is typically the most population-based and regionally detailed studies [N1-F1][N1-F2][N3-F3][N6-R5].

Radiation/environmental influences and diagnostic bias are important drivers of observed pediatric thyroid cancer incidence, but the evidence suggests that these factors are often confounded and not easily separated. The strongest direct evidence for radiation-related pediatric thyroid cancer incidence comes from cohort studies and reviews showing that even small doses of ionizing radiation can increase the risk of childhood thyroid cancer, with a linear dose-response up to 10–20 Gy [N6-R2]. A pooled analysis of nine cohort studies of childhood external radiation exposure reaffirmed a linear increase in thyroid cancer risk, supporting the idea that radiation exposure is a real cause [N6-R4]. The broader global pediatric thyroid cancer burden article also states that the primary risk factors for children and adolescents include exposure to significant levels of ionizing radiation [N6-R3]. Together, these sources provide strong evidence that radiation exposure can increase pediatric thyroid cancer incidence.

Imaging and detection bias also play a major role. The CDC pediatric cancer report explicitly states that increased use of medical imaging may lead to geographic differences in thyroid cancer incidence via enhanced detection of low-risk lesions, often as incidental findings [N3-R4]. The population-based childhood study similarly notes that the pattern of incidence in children and adolescents mirrors the pattern seen in adults, suggesting a major role for overdiagnosis [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN report also notes that the widespread use of imaging techniques and fine-needle aspiration biopsy has improved detection of thyroid cancer and raised concerns about overdiagnosis [N1-F1]. These points indicate that observed incidence increases may partly reflect better detection rather than a true increase in disease burden.

Environmental exposure beyond radiation is also relevant. The global pediatric thyroid cancer burden article states that environmental exposure is a primary risk factor, though the excerpt does not specify which exposures [N6-R3]. The N1-F2 study notes that the variability in incidence rates was mostly accounted for by the papillary tumor subtype, which implies that tumor biology and environmental exposures may interact to shape incidence patterns [N1-F2]. The N4 evidence, while not specifically about environmental exposure, supports the idea that incidence trends can be influenced by improved detection and changing clinical practice [N4-R1].

These factors affect observed geographic variation in several ways. First, radiation exposure can create localized or regional increases in incidence, especially in areas with a history of childhood radiation exposure [N6-R2][N6-R4]. Second, better access to imaging and biopsies can create geographic differences because some regions may detect thyroid cancer more readily than others [N3-R4][N1-F2]. Third, environmental exposure may vary by region, contributing to regional differences in incidence [N6-R3]. Fourth, overdiagnosis and improved detection can amplify apparent geographic variation, making it difficult to distinguish true biological variation from ascertainment variation [N1-F2][N1-F1][N3-R4].

In summary, the evidence supports radiation and environmental factors as important determinants of pediatric thyroid cancer incidence, but it also shows that diagnostic bias, imaging use, and improved detection can greatly inflate observed incidence and create geographic variation that is not entirely attributable to biology [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N3-R4][N1-F2].

## How does the incidence of pediatric thyroid cancer vary by age, gender, and geographic region?

The evidence shows that pediatric thyroid cancer incidence is shaped by age, gender, and geography, but the picture is best understood as a combination of biological trends, environmental factors, and diagnostic influences. Across the branch reports, the strongest overall conclusion is that incidence rises with age, is higher in girls than boys, and varies widely by region, with some areas showing much higher rates than others [N1-F2][N1-F1][N1-F1][N1-R2][N3-F3].

---

## 1) Age-specific patterns: incidence rises with age, especially in adolescents

Pediatric thyroid cancer incidence is generally lowest in infancy and increases with age, with the strongest evidence pointing to a rise in older children and adolescents. The population-based study of children and adolescents aged 0–19 years reports that incidence rates were almost always higher in girls than in boys and increased with age in both sexes [N1-F2]. This suggests a broad upward trend across childhood age groups.

In the youngest age group, evidence is less precise than in older children, but the CDC pediatric cancer report notes that pediatric cancer incidence was highest in children aged 0–4 years overall, while in some states the highest rates were among persons aged 15–19 years [N3-F3]. This implies that infants and very young children may have relatively lower rates compared with older children and adolescents, but the evidence does not support a simple “peak” in infancy. Instead, the pattern is better described as lowest in infancy, increasing in children, and rising further in adolescents [N1-F2][N3-F3].

The broader global and national evidence also supports this age pattern. The 2021 global data highlight that the 20–24 age group bears a substantial thyroid cancer burden, while the U.S. evidence notes that thyroid cancer incidence increased across all age groups from 1995 to 2014, including in the 0–14 and 15–24 groups [N1-R2][N4-R1]. Taken together, the most reliable evidence base for age patterns is the population-based childhood study and the broader incidence evidence, which both support a generally increasing trend with age [N1-F2][N1-R2][N4-R1].

A key caveat is that the population-based childhood study notes that incidence rates were strongly correlated with adult rates and that temporal increases were observed almost everywhere, which suggests that the apparent age pattern may be influenced by secular trends rather than purely biological age effects [N1-F2]. Still, the age-specific pattern itself remains consistent: incidence rises with age, with the steepest increases occurring in adolescents and young adults, and the lowest rates in infancy or the youngest age groups [N1-F2][N3-F3].

## 2) Gender differences: girls consistently have higher incidence than boys

Gender differences are consistent across the evidence. The population-based childhood study reports that incidence rates were almost always higher in girls than in boys [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN 2022 global cancer report similarly states that thyroid cancer is three to four times more common in women than in men and that the female-to-male age-standardized incidence rate ratio ranges from 3 to 4 depending on the country analyzed [N1-F1]. The Frontiers in Oncology article on pediatric and adolescent thyroid cancer also notes that women account for a large proportion of cases and that the female-to-male incidence ratio is substantial [N1-R2].

The possible explanations for the gender gap are primarily biological. The GLOBOCAN report explicitly links the higher incidence in women to biological factors and states that thyroid cancer is the only non-reproductive cancer that predominantly affects women [N1-F1]. The same report also notes that the female excess is “three to four times” greater than in men, which is consistent with hormonal and other biological mechanisms [N1-F1]. The pediatric cancer geography report does not specifically discuss thyroid cancer gender differences, so it is not directly relevant to this point [N3-F3].

As for whether the gender gap changes with age, the evidence is more nuanced. The population-based childhood study states that incidence increases with age in both sexes, but it does not provide evidence that the female excess becomes larger or smaller with age [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN report likewise states that the female-to-male incidence ratio is consistent across regions and that the female excess is a major feature of thyroid cancer epidemiology [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic/Medscape summaries also note that women are three to four times more likely than men to be diagnosed with thyroid cancer, reinforcing the gender gap [N2-R5].

So, the most reliable conclusion is that girls consistently have higher incidence than boys, and the gender gap appears to be relatively stable across age groups, though the evidence does not support a strong change in the gap with age [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R5].

---

## 3) Geographic variation: substantial regional and country-level differences

Geographic variation is substantial, but the evidence base is uneven. The strongest direct evidence comes from the population-based childhood study, which reports age-standardized incidence rates ranging from 0.4 to 13.4 per 1 million person-years in 49 countries and territories, with the highest rate observed in Belarus and the lowest in Uganda and Kenya [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN 2022 report adds that age-standardized incidence rates in high HDI countries were approximately ten times higher than those in low HDI countries for both sexes [N1-F1]. This implies a major geographic gradient, with higher incidence in wealthier regions.

Within the United States, the CDC pediatric cancer report indicates that pediatric cancer incidence was highest in the Northeast and lowest in the South, with highest rates in metropolitan areas with populations ≥1 million and counties in the top 25% economic status [N3-F3]. The same report notes that incidence rates ranged from 145 to 206 per million and were highest in New Hampshire, the District of Columbia, and New Jersey [N3-F3]. It also shows that incidence rates vary by state, Census region, and county-level economic status, suggesting that incidence differs by continent, country, and urban/rural setting [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence does not provide continent-specific country-level data in the branch reports, but the incidence range of 0.4–13.4 per million person-years already suggests large variation across countries and regions [N1-F2]. The CDC report also provides the clearest urban/rural distinction, noting higher rates in metropolitan areas than in nonmetropolitan areas [N3-F3]. Taken together, the geographic patterns suggest that incidence differs by continent, country, and urban/rural setting, with high HDI regions showing much higher incidence than low HDI regions [N1-F1][N3-F3].

---

## 4) Possible explanations for geographic variation

The geographic variation is best interpreted as a combination of real biological and environmental factors, plus diagnostic and detection-related factors.

### Environmental and radiation exposure
The evidence suggests that radiation exposure is an important determinant. Cohort studies and reviews show that even small doses of ionizing radiation can increase the risk of childhood thyroid cancer, with a linear dose-response up to 10–20 Gy [N6-R2]. A pooled analysis of nine cohort studies of childhood external radiation exposure reaffirmed a linear increase in thyroid cancer risk, supporting the idea that radiation exposure is a real cause [N6-R4]. The global pediatric thyroid cancer burden article also states that the primary risk factors for children and adolescents include exposure to significant levels of ionizing radiation [N6-R3]. Together, these sources provide strong evidence that radiation exposure can increase pediatric thyroid cancer incidence.

### Imaging, detection bias, and improved diagnosis
Imaging and detection bias also play a major role. The CDC pediatric cancer report explicitly states that increased use of medical imaging may lead to geographic differences in thyroid cancer incidence via enhanced detection of low-risk lesions, often as incidental findings [N3-R4]. The population-based childhood study similarly notes that the pattern of incidence in children and adolescents mirrors the pattern seen in adults, suggesting a major role for overdiagnosis [N1-F2]. The GLOBOCAN report also notes that the widespread use of imaging techniques and fine-needle aspiration biopsy has improved detection of thyroid cancer and raised concerns about overdiagnosis [N1-F1]. These points indicate that observed incidence increases may partly reflect better detection rather than a true increase in disease burden.

### Environmental exposure beyond radiation
The global pediatric thyroid cancer burden article states that environmental exposure is a primary risk factor, though the excerpt does not specify which exposures [N6-R3]. The population-based childhood study notes that the variability in incidence rates was mostly accounted for by the papillary tumor subtype, which implies that tumor biology and environmental exposures may interact to shape incidence patterns [N1-F2].

### Implications for geographic variation
These factors affect observed geographic variation in several ways. First, radiation exposure can create localized or regional increases in incidence, especially in areas with a history of childhood radiation exposure [N6-R2][N6-R4]. Second, better access to imaging and biopsies can create geographic differences because some regions may detect thyroid cancer more readily than others [N3-R4][N1-F2]. Third, environmental exposure may vary by region, contributing to regional differences in incidence [N6-R3]. Fourth, overdiagnosis and improved detection can amplify apparent geographic variation, making it difficult to distinguish true biological variation from ascertainment variation [N1-F2][N1-F1][N3-R4].

---

## 5) Study quality and limitations

Registry methods, case ascertainment, and diagnostic criteria affect estimates. The GLOBOCAN report states that the reliability of cancer data at the national level depends on the representativeness and quality of the source information, and that the methods used in compiling cancer estimates are consistent with those used in previous studies [N1-F1]. The same report notes that national cancer registries and vital registries provided the best available recorded data, while the reliability of data depends on source quality [N1-F1]. The population-based childhood study similarly uses population-based cancer data from the International Incidence of Childhood Cancer Volume 3 study, the WHO mortality database, and the CI5plus database, which implies that these data are intended to be high-quality but still subject to registry limitations [N1-F2].

Diagnostic criteria and age/gender definitions also vary across studies. The population-based childhood study reports age-standardized incidence rates and uses person-years of follow-up, which is a standard method for incidence estimation [N1-F2]. However, the GLOBOCAN report explicitly notes that incidence rates were higher in women than in men and that the female-to-male ASIR ratio varies by country, indicating that age and sex definitions may not be identical across all studies [N1-F1]. The CDC pediatric cancer report likewise uses age-adjusted rates and reports incidence by sex, race/ethnicity, state, Census region, and county-level economic status [N3-F3]. The U.S. incidence evidence also notes that incidence increased across all age groups from 1995 to 2014, but it does not provide enough detail on diagnostic criteria for thyroid cancer specifically [N4-R1]. The radiation/environmental evidence adds that imaging and radiation exposure may contribute to increased incidence, which is relevant to case ascertainment but not directly to diagnostic criteria [N6-R5].

The most reliable evidence base for each subgroup is therefore uneven. For age patterns, the population-based childhood study provides the strongest direct evidence, because it is explicitly population-based and covers children and adolescents aged 0–19 years [N1-F2]. For gender differences, the GLOBOCAN report and the Frontiers in Oncology article provide the most reliable cross-population evidence, because they report age-standardized incidence ratios and global patterns [N1-F1][N1-R2]. For geographic variation, the CDC pediatric cancer report is the most reliable regional and country-level source because it provides state-level estimates and detailed geographic breakdowns [N3-F3]. For radiation and environmental influences, the N6 evidence is strongest because it directly links radiation exposure and imaging to thyroid cancer incidence [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

---

## 6) Integrated conclusion

Overall, the incidence of pediatric thyroid cancer varies in three main ways:

- **By age:** incidence is lowest in infancy, increases with age, and rises most steeply in adolescents and young adults [N1-F2][N3-F3][N4-R1].
- **By gender:** incidence is consistently higher in girls than in boys, with a female excess that appears stable across age groups [N1-F2][N1-F1][N2-R5].
- **By geography:** incidence varies substantially by region, country, and urban/rural setting, with high HDI regions showing much higher rates than low HDI regions and some U.S. areas showing especially high rates [N1-F1][N3-F3].

The evidence also shows that these patterns are not entirely biological. Radiation exposure can increase incidence, while improved imaging, detection bias, and overdiagnosis can inflate observed rates and create geographic variation that may reflect ascertainment rather than true biological variation [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N3-R4][N1-F1]. Therefore, the most cautious interpretation is that pediatric thyroid cancer incidence is shaped by a combination of age, gender, geography, radiation, environmental exposure, and diagnostic factors, with the most reliable evidence coming from population-based studies and regionally detailed registries [N1-F2][N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R5].
